{{Short description|Type of conserved current}}
In [[particle physics]], the '''axial current''', also denoted the ''pseudo-vector'' or ''chiral'' current, is the [[conserved current]] associated to the [[chiral symmetry]] or [[axial symmetry]] of a system.

== Origin ==

According to [[Noether's theorem]], each [[symmetry]] of a system is associated a conserved quantity.<ref>
{{cite arXiv |eprint=physics/9807044 |first=Nina |last=Byers|title=E. Noether's Discovery of the Deep Connection Between Symmetries and Conservation Laws |year=1998 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Baez |first1=John  |author-link1=John Baez |title=Noether's Theorem in a Nutshell |url=https://math.ucr.edu/home/baez/noether.html |website=math.ucr.edu |access-date=28 August 2020 |date=2002}}</ref> For example, the [[rotational invariance]] of a system implies the conservation of its [[angular momentum]], or spacetime invariance implies the conservation of energy–momentum. In [[quantum field theory]], [[internal symmetries]] also result in conserved quantities. For example, the [[U(1)]] [[gauge invariance]] of [[Quantum electrodynamics|QED]] implies the conservation of the [[electric charge]]. Likewise, if a theory possesses an internal chiral or axial symmetry, there will be a conserved quantity, which is called the '''''axial charge'''''. Further, just as the motion of an electrically charged particle produces an [[electric current]], a moving axial charge constitutes an axial current.

== Definition ==
The axial current resulting from the motion of an axially charged moving particle is formally defined as  <math>j_5^\mu = \overline\psi\gamma^5\gamma^\mu\psi</math>, where  <math> \psi </math> is the [[Field (physics)|particle field]] represented by [[Dirac spinor]] (since the particle is typically a [[Spin (physics)|spin]]-1/2 [[fermion]]) and <math> \gamma^5 </math> and <math> \gamma^\mu </math> are the [[Dirac]] [[gamma matrices]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Zee |first=A. |title=Quantum Field Theory in a Nutshell: Second Edition |title-link=Quantum Field Theory in a Nutshell |date=2010-02-01 |publisher=Princeton University Press |isbn=978-1-4008-3532-4 |pages=100 |language=en |author-link=Anthony Zee}}</ref>

For comparison, the electromagnetic current produced by an electrically charged moving particle is  <math>j^\mu = \overline\psi\gamma^\mu\psi</math>.

== Meaning ==
As explained above, the axial current is simply the equivalent of the electromagnetic current for the axial symmetry instead of the U(1) symmetry. Another perspective is given by recalling that the 
[[chiral symmetry]] is the [[Invariant (physics)|invariance]] of the theory under the field rotation <math>\psi_{\rm L}\rightarrow e^{i\theta_{\rm L}}\psi_{\rm L}</math>&nbsp;&nbsp;and&nbsp;&nbsp;<math>\psi_{\rm R}\rightarrow \psi_{\rm R}</math> (or alternatively <math>\psi_{\rm L}\rightarrow \psi_{\rm L}</math>&nbsp;&nbsp;and&nbsp;&nbsp; <math>\psi_{\rm R}\rightarrow e^{i\theta_{\rm R}}\psi_{\rm R}</math>), where <math>\psi_{\rm L}</math> denotes a [[Helicity (particle physics)|left-handed field]] and <math>\psi_{\rm R}</math> a right-handed one. 
From this as well as the fact that <math>\psi=\psi_{\rm L}+\psi_{\rm R}</math> and the definition of <math>j_5^\mu </math> above, one sees that the axial current is the difference between the current due to left-handed fermions and that from right-handed ones, whilst the electromagnetic current is the sum.

Chiral symmetry is exhibited by vector [[gauge theory|gauge theories]] with massless fermions. Since there is no known massless fermion in nature, chiral symmetry is at best an approximate symmetry in fundamental theories, and the axial current is not conserved. (Note: this [[explicit symmetry breaking|explicit breaking]] of the chiral symmetry by non-zero masses is not to be confused with the [[spontaneous symmetry breaking|spontaneous]] [[chiral symmetry breaking]] that plays a dominant role in [[hadron|hadronic physics]].) An important consequence of such non-conservation is the neutral [[pion]] [[Particle decay|decay]] and the [[chiral anomaly]],<ref>
{{cite journal
 |last1=Dolgov |first1=A. D.
 |year=1997
 |title=Baryogenesis, 30 years after
 |journal=[[Surveys in High Energy Physics]]
 |volume=13 |issue=1–3 |pages=83–117
 |arxiv=hep-ph/9707419
 |bibcode=1998SHEP...13...83D
 |doi=10.1080/01422419808240874
|s2cid=119499400
 }}</ref> which is directly related to the pion [[Relativistic Breit–Wigner distribution|decay width]].<ref name=Adler>
{{cite journal
 |last1=Adler |first1=S. L.
 |year=1969
 |title=Axial-Vector Vertex in Spinor Electrodynamics
 |journal=[[Physical Review]]
 |volume=177 |issue=5 |pages=2426–2438

}}
</ref><ref name=bj>

== Applications ==

The axial current is an important part of the formalism describing [[high-energy physics|high-energy scattering]] reactions. In such reaction, two particles scatter off each other by exchanging a force [[vector boson|boson]], e.g., a [[photon]] for electromagnetic scattering (see the figure). 
[[Image:Electron-scattering.png|thumb|220px|A [[Feynman diagram]] of scattering between two electrons by emission of a virtual [[photon]].]]
The [[Cross section (physics)|cross-section]] for such reaction is proportional to the square of the [[scattering amplitude]], which in turn is given by the product of boson [[propagator]] times the two currents associated with the motions two colliding particles.<ref name="peskin">
{{cite book
 |last1=Peskin |first1=M.
 |author-link=Michael Peskin
 |last2=Schroeder |first2=D.
 |year=1995
 |title=An Introduction to Quantum Field Theory
 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=i35LALN0GosC
 |publisher=Westview Press
 |isbn=978-0-201-50397-5 }}</ref> Therefore, currents (axial or electromagnetic) are one of the two essential ingredients needed to compute [[high-energy physics|high-energy scattering]], the other being the boson [[propagator]].

In electron–nucleon [[scattering]] (or more generally, charged [[lepton]]–[[hadron]]/[[Atomic nucleus|nucleus]] scattering) the axial current yields the [[Spin (physics)|spin]]-dependent part of the [[Cross section (physics)|cross-section]].<ref name="SR review">[https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.05250 A. Deur, S. J. Brodsky, G. F. de Teramond (2019) “The Spin Structure of the Nucleon”] Rept. Prog. Phys. 82 076201</ref> (The spin-average part of the cross-section comes from the electromagnetic current.<ref name="peskin"/>)

In [[neutrino]]–nucleon scattering, neutrinos couple only via the axial current, thus accessing different nucleon structure information than with charged leptons.<ref name="Zuber">
{{cite book
 |last=Zuber
 |first=Kai
 |year=2020
 |title=Neutrino Physics
 |publisher=CRC Press
 |isbn=9781315195612
 |url=https://doi.org/10.1201/9781315195612}}</ref>

Neutral [[pion]]s also couple only via the axial current because pions are [[pseudoscalar]] particles and, to produce amplitudes (scalar quantities), a pion must couple to another pseudoscalar object like the axial current. (Charged pions can also couple via the electromagnetic current.)
